content: When the approved sample size for a survey has been reached or the allocated budget has been exhausted, survey staff should courteously inform individuals seeking participation about the situation. A standardized script should be developed to assist staff in effectively communicating this message to potential participants. Survey sites will remain open for scheduled follow-up visits, and eligible participants presenting valid coupons during this time should be reimbursed for transportation costs, even if they are not enrolled in the survey. Monitoring is an ongoing activity throughout the survey and contributes to improved data quality. It should be conducted by survey staff and investigators, with documentation of monitoring activities to enhance current and future surveys. Key areas for monitoring include interviewer performance, adherence to SOPs, proper sampling, participant recruitment, and data collection. During enrollment, it is essential to confirm that participant consent is properly administered and that ineligible individuals are not enrolled. Data collection should be conducted in adequate spaces, and any issues with missing interviews or problematic questionnaire items should be addressed. Supervisors should also verify that qualitative interviews sufficiently probe key themes and that audio recordings, if used, are of adequate quality for transcription. Feedback from participants can be obtained through direct approaches or anonymous suggestion boxes. Laboratory monitoring should include observing 10% of specimen collections, with increased frequency (25%) at the beginning of the survey. Supervisors should conduct regular checks to identify and correct issues such as hemolyzed blood specimens, improperly dried blood spots, illegible or missing labels, and inadequate specimen storage. Data preparation for analysis involves cleaning, merging, and assessing data quality. Errors should be resolved systematically, with documentation of all corrections in a data-audit log. Missing data should be minimized as much as possible, as it can affect the reliability and validity of survey results. Investigators should distinguish between different types of missing responses, such as don’t know or refused to answer, and document reasons for missing data. Imputation methods, such as multiple imputation, may be used to address missing values, but these require consultation with a statistician. When appending datasets from multiple sources, variable names and definitions should remain consistent. Any changes to the data collection tool or questionnaire should be documented, and a new version of the tool should be saved.
